actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Ms. Clara Bennett, and today we'll start our journey into HTML, the building blocks of every web page.

First, HTML is the foundation of web pages—it gives structure to everything you see online. In this lesson we'll cover three main objectives: understanding document structure, learning a handful of basic tags, and picking up best practices for clean, readable code. We'll also see how long each part will take and try a few quick interactive activities along the way.
By the end of today, you’ll be able to write a simple HTML page, identify the key elements, and feel confident adding your own content.
Let's get started and have some fun building the web together!

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Ms. Clara Bennett, and today we're going to build the foundation of every web page—the basic HTML document structure.
First, let's talk about the essential elements that make up a valid HTML page. These are the building blocks that browsers expect to see.
Notice the DOCTYPE declaration at the very top—<!DOCTYPE html>. This tells the browser that we are using HTML5, the modern standard.
Below that, we have the root <html> element, which contains two child sections: <head> for metadata and <body> for the content that appears on the page.

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Clara, and today we’ll explore how to add links and images to our web pages.
First, let’s create a hyperlink. We use the <a> tag with an href attribute that points to the URL we want to link to.
Here’s a simple example: Visit Example. When users click this text, they’ll be taken to the specified site.
Next, to display an image we use the tag with src for the image file and alt for alternative text. The alt text is important for accessibility.
Finally, we can combine both by wrapping an tag inside an tag—this creates a clickable image that leads to another page.
Remember, always provide meaningful alt text for images so everyone can understand what the picture represents.

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into today’s topic: Lists and Tables in HTML.
First, we have ordered lists, created with the <ol> tag, and unordered lists, created with <ul>. Both use <li> for each list item.
Think of an ordered list like a numbered recipe step‑by‑step, while an unordered list is more like a simple checklist.
Now, let’s look at tables. A table starts with <table>, rows are defined with <tr>, headers with <th>, and regular cells with <td>.
Putting it all together, a basic list and a simple table can be written in just a few lines of HTML – a great way to organize information on a web page.
That covers the essentials for today. Feel free to try creating your own list and table, and we’ll review any questions together.

questions.question: Which tag correctly defines the largest heading in an HTML document?
questions.analysis: The <h1> tag defines the top-level heading. <title> is for the browser tab title, <head> encloses metadata, and <header> is a sectioning element, not a heading.

questions.question: Select all tags that are required for a minimal valid HTML5 document (select all that apply).
questions.analysis: A complete HTML5 document needs <html>, <head> (which must contain a <title>), and <body>. All four tags are essential for validity.

questions.question: Explain the difference between the <section> and <div> elements and give one example of when to use each.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Describes <section> as a semantic grouping with a thematic purpose – 40% (2) Describes <div> as a generic container without semantic meaning – 30% (3) Provides a clear example for each – 30%
questions.analysis: A good answer states that <section> groups related content with its own heading (e.g., a news article's 'Related Stories' section), while <div> is used purely for styling or layout when no semantic meaning is needed (e.g., a wrapper for a grid layout).

actions.text: Now let's check what we've learned about basic HTML elements. This short quiz will help you see if you can identify the right tags and understand how they fit together in a document.

Remember, the largest heading tag is <h1>, and a minimal HTML5 page needs the <html>, <head>, <title>, and <body> elements. For the upcoming short‑answer question, think about how <section> groups related content with its own heading, while <div> is just a generic container for styling or scripting.

Take your time with each question, read the options carefully, and try to apply the examples we discussed earlier. If anything feels unclear, don't worry—you'll get a chance to review the explanations right after you submit your answers.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML and why good practices matter for every web page we build.
First, these semantic tags—header, nav, main, section, article, and footer—give meaning to the structure of our pages. Browsers, screen readers, and search engines all understand them better.
Because they describe *what* the content is, accessibility tools can navigate more easily, and search engines can rank our pages higher.
Beyond tags, remember to keep your code tidy: use proper indentation, choose meaningful class names, and always add alt attributes for images.
Finally, run through a quick checklist—semantic tags in place, clean indentation, descriptive classes, and alt text—to ensure your HTML is both readable and accessible. Great job, everyone!

questions.question: Which HTML5 semantic element is most appropriate for enclosing the main navigation links of a website?
questions.analysis: The <nav> element is specifically designed to contain a set of navigation links. <section> groups related content, <aside> holds tangential content, and <footer> contains footer information.

questions.question: Select all statements that describe good HTML coding practices (choose all that apply).

options.label: Including presentational styling directly in HTML attributes
Providing descriptive alt text for images

questions.analysis: Good practices include lowercase tags, proper indentation, and meaningful alt attributes. Inline presentational styling should be avoided in favor of CSS.

actions.text: Alright, let's take a quick final check on what we just covered about semantic HTML and clean coding habits.
Remember, each HTML5 element has a specific purpose. Choosing the right tag helps both browsers and users understand the structure of your page.

For example, the <nav> element is designed especially for groups of navigation links, while <section> groups related content, <aside> holds tangential information, and <footer> marks the bottom of a page. Picking the correct one keeps your markup meaningful.

Good coding practices include using lowercase tag names, indenting nested elements for readability, and always providing descriptive alt text for images. Adding presentational styling directly in HTML attributes, like inline style or bgcolor, is discouraged because it mixes content with design.
